doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

title: Jazz in academia versus the blues
summary: Why jazz entered universities, his NEA start in 1977, and loss of individual voices.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Where does blues fit in the art forms that we are so, they are so much a part of American culture. As I said before, you can now get a Ph.D. in jazz studies but there are no such levels of academia that focus on the blues. Do you know if there’s a reason for that?

Well the fact that I think that jazz musicians have been more aggressive and challenging the institutions, to incorporate them. And blues musicians have not had that kind of orientation. They have not based them in academic people and whereas jazz musicians in the latter part of the twentieth century were more academically inclined. And once you started getting like, and communities demanded it too. Like for example the demand for black studies in the 1960s would lead to the establishment of jazz programs because that’s something that a university could do to address its omission of African-American cultural development, including African-American history within its curricula. And also there was more of a faculty to be had. So yes I mean I think — I very much remember the way it was when I first went to the National Endowment for the Arts in 1977. At that time jazz was considered to be commercial music, completely unworthy of being addressed by cultural institutions including universities. It belonged outside of it. It’s a large part of jazz’s history as you know, which has always been outside of history up until again this current age. So once you started getting jazz programs established some of the early programs like the one at North Texas State, which developed a really good jazz orchestra, didn’t have many black people in it but it did at least recognize the music and showed that you could have a serious academic curriculum that could develop the music. Once that momentum started then of course it spread to where every conservatory had to have some kind of a jazz program. Now it hasn’t been altogether a great thing, because again, something gets lost when you make these big social based transformations in the music. We now have more — this generation of jazz musicians, which has more technique, knows more theory and more history than any other, and yet it’s you almost can’t tell them apart, the products of these things. Something gets lost when you have to make these discoveries of the instrument on your own without being told how to play it by a professor. Maybe an older musician on the instrument will give you some tips every now and then but basically you had to find it yourself. But in so doing you do develop a voice and you develop a sound. So the generations of musicians where you hear a phrase of Ben Webster and know it’s Ben Webster, you know what I mean, that is gone. Also I find it odd that with all these musicians, again more technically adept, more theoretically sound than any other generation, we haven’t had an overriding genius appear since John Coltrane. And he died in 1967. That’s 55 years ago. Coltrane and Charlie Parker overlapped. You know? Louis Armstrong and Charlie Parker overlapped. You know? Art Tatum overlapped with bebop musicians. But, so it’s in a strange place. I don’t really understand where it goes or how it goes but maybe —
